1533: Six components returned eigenvalues exceeding unity and together accounted for 83.82% of the total variation. The first two alone accounted for 50.61% and the first three for 62.99%. The scree plot in Figure 4.2 exhibits the sharp inflexion after the second component, the customary indication that the first two carry the greater part of the informative variation.
1534: The first component explained 31.23% of the variation and returned an eigenvalue of 7.184. It loaded heavily and positively on aroma (+0.939), antioxidant capacity (+0.910), total phenol (+0.893), fat (+0.881), total flavonoid (+0.871) and soluble protein (+0.805), and heavily and negatively on amylose (-0.713) and total colour difference (-0.604). This constitutes the storage axis: every trait declining during storage loads positively and every trait rising loads negatively. Reading the biplot in Figure 4.3 from right to left is therefore equivalent to reading the storage period from fresh paddy to twelve months.
1535: The second component explained 19.37% of the variation and returned an eigenvalue of 4.456. It loaded most heavily and positively on phytic acid (+0.898), iron (+0.481) and L* (+0.461), and negatively on head rice recovery (-0.755), a* (-0.621), ash (-0.563) and amylose (-0.562). This represents largely a varietal axis: Gobindabhog, carrying the most phytic acid and the most iron, is positioned high on this component, whereas Kalojira, with the best head rice recovery and the most ash, is positioned low.
1536: The third component explained 12.39% and separated the minerals from the remaining characters, loading positively on zinc (+0.868) and copper (+0.789) and negatively on manganese (-0.747). Since storage exerted no effect on any of the minerals, this component evidently captures differences between locations in soil mineral supply.
1537: The biplot in Figure 4.3 renders the structure readily interpretable. The twelve Kalojira points cluster together to the right and low, denoting high aroma, high phenolic content and high head rice recovery. Within each landrace the four storage points run from right to left in sequence, from fresh paddy through to twelve months, the length of that trajectory indicating the magnitude of change in the landrace. The vectors for aroma, fat, phenol, flavonoid and antioxidant capacity are co-directional and closely apposed, confirming the tight correlation already noted. The amylose vector points in the opposite direction, and the phytic acid vector lies nearly orthogonal to both groups, which indicates that phytic acid varies independently of the aroma and phenolic complex.
1538: The practical value of this analysis lies in its reduction of twenty three separate determinations to two interpretable dimensions capturing half the variation between them. A treatment may be located on the biplot and its entire quality profile read off at a glance, which is considerably more expeditious than comparing twenty three tables in succession.
1544: Hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on the standardised data using Ward's minimum variance method with Euclidean distance. This method amalgamates the most similar treatments and constructs a tree, presented as the dendrogram in Figure 4.4. The cophenetic correlation was 0.503, a moderate value indicating that the tree affords a fair though not exact representation of the distances between treatments.
1545: Cutting the tree into four groups yielded clusters of 12, 4, 7 and 13 treatments. The salient feature is that the grouping follows the landrace far more closely than it follows either location or storage period.
1546: Cluster 1 comprised precisely the twelve Kalojira treatments and nothing further, that is, all three locations at all four storage periods. No Kalojira treatment fell outside it and no other landrace fell within it. This cluster returned the highest aroma (2.51), the highest total phenol (0.7812 mg GAE/g), the highest antioxidant capacity (40.26 mg TE/100 g), the highest head rice recovery (67.07%), the highest hulling (77.52%) and the lowest phytic acid (196.07 mg/100 g). It is the superior cluster on almost every consequential count, and it is defined purely by genotype.
1547: Cluster 2 comprised the four Radhunipagal treatments from Nadia. Small and tightly defined, it is distinguished by mineral content rather than by any other attribute, returning much the highest zinc at 1.37 ppm, nearly three times the level of the other clusters, together with the highest ash at 1.16% and the highest copper. This demonstrates that one landrace at one location may behave quite unlike the same landrace elsewhere, which constitutes the clearest possible confirmation of the location × variety interactions reported throughout this chapter.
1548: Cluster 3 comprised seven treatments, all of them Gobindabhog or Radhunipagal from the intermediate and later storage periods, predominantly from Purba Bardhaman. This is the deteriorated group, returning the lowest aroma (1.78), the lowest total phenol (0.4380 mg GAE/g), the lowest antioxidant capacity (22.33 mg TE/100 g) and the lowest ash. It illustrates the outcome where a landrace of only moderate initial quality is grown at the weakest location and subsequently held for eight to twelve months.
1549: Cluster 4 comprised thirteen treatments, consisting principally of fresh and early-stored Gobindabhog together with the earlier Radhunipagal samples. It returned the highest phytic acid at 373.41 mg/100 g and the highest iron at 0.48 ppm, with intermediate values for most other traits.
1550: Three inferences emerge from the clustering. First, genotype constituted the strongest single determinant of overall quality, Kalojira separating completely from the other two landraces before any further division appeared in the tree. Second, storage was the next strongest determinant, since within Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal the fresh and early samples separated from the late ones. Third, location mattered least of the three overall, yet proved decisive in the single case of Radhunipagal at Nadia, which resolved into a cluster of its own on the strength of its mineral content.
1551: For a breeding or marketing programme the implication is unambiguous. Kalojira should be selected for aroma, phenolics and milling outturn, and Radhunipagal from Nadia where mineral content is the objective. Gobindabhog and Radhunipagal from Purba Bardhaman should not be held beyond eight months, that being the combination which falls into the poorest cluster.
1555: The place of production proved influential for nearly every trait measured. Birbhum and Howrah returned the best milling percentage, head rice recovery, total phenol, total flavonoid, antioxidant capacity, iron and phytic acid. Nadia returned the best hulling, soluble protein, fat, copper and zinc. Purba Bardhaman was the weakest location for the majority of traits determining nutritional value.
1556: Kalojira emerged as the superior all-round landrace, ranking highest for hulling, milling, head rice recovery, total starch, amylose, fat, ash, aroma, total phenol, total flavonoid and antioxidant capacity. Gobindabhog was superior for soluble protein, grain shape, iron and thirteen of the fifteen amino acids. Radhunipagal ranked highest for zinc alone and was the poorest performer for most milling and nutritional traits.
1557: Storage acted upon quality in two opposing directions concurrently. Milling improved as the grain aged, head rice recovery gaining 2.13 percentage points up to 8 months and amylose increasing by 12.8% over the year. Against these gains, aroma declined by 31.7%, soluble protein by 41.4%, fat by 31.3%, total phenol by 52.4%, total flavonoid by 37.3% and antioxidant capacity by 62.7%.
1558: Copper, iron, zinc and manganese remained unchanged throughout storage, while phytic acid declined by 40.0% over the same period. Since phytic acid is the constituent impeding absorption of iron and zinc, the balance between them improved progressively as the grain aged. Aged grain may therefore be expected to release its minerals more readily than fresh grain, notwithstanding that it contains no greater quantity of them.
1559: The interactions yield three inferences that the main effects alone would conceal. First, for the milling traits and for aroma the order of the landraces was conserved at every location, so that the choice of landrace may be made once for the whole of West Bengal. Second, for soluble protein, ash and all four minerals the order of the landraces varied from location to location, so that no landrace can be recommended for these traits without specification of the district. Third, for aroma, fat and amylose all three landraces changed at nearly identical rates during storage, which implies that a single storage regime will serve all of them.
1560: Taken together, a storage period of four to eight months represents the optimal compromise for these landraces. Within that window the greater part of the milling gain conferred by ageing has been secured while the loss of aroma and health-promoting compounds remains moderate. Holding the grain beyond eight months under ambient conditions forfeits a substantial proportion of the aroma and antioxidant value for which these landraces command a premium, and none of it is recoverable.
1568: The seven products in this experiment were prepared from nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal, with Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar, included as the control. Each product was laid out in a completely randomised design with three replications and repeated over two years. The two years were analysed jointly as a pooled design, with year as a fixed effect and cultivar as a random effect. The model was Yijk = μ + Yi + Tj + (YT)ij + eijk, the degrees of freedom being year 1, cultivar 9, year × cultivar 9, error 40 and total 59.
1569: The results are presented in two parts: Part A covers the four cooked products, namely table rice, khichdi, pulao and payash, and Part B the three processed products, namely popped rice, puffed rice and flattened rice. Within each part every attribute is presented once for the group, with all the products of that part assembled in one table and one figure, both reporting the means pooled over the two years. Means were separated at the 5% level and are reported with letter groupings; a cultivar is deemed to differ from the control only where the two share no letter. Throughout, ** denotes significance at 1%, * at 5% and NS non-significance. Since a high value is favourable for certain attributes and a low value for others, each cultivar is compared with the control in the direction appropriate to that attribute.
1570: Each part concludes with a composite quality score index, a verification of the weights of that index by principal component analysis, a cluster analysis of the cultivar and product combinations, and a conclusion. Tables and figures are numbered consecutively through both parts.
1576: Amylose content determines the firmness and discreteness of the cooked grain: a higher content yields a firmer, drier grain that retains its shape, and a lower content a softer, stickier one. In table rice the values ranged from 15.63 in Harinakhuri to 19.82% in Kalojira. The control recorded 17.19%, 8 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalojira proved the most favourable. Tulaipanji recorded the highest value in khichdi at 9.11% and Kalonunia the lowest at 6.14%; against 6.77% for the control, 3 cultivars exceeded it, Tulaipanji being the most favourable entry. For pulao the values lay between 16.30 and 20.57%, with the control at 18.35%; here 2 cultivars exceeded the control, Kalojira ranking highest. In payash the values ranged from 16.74 in Harinakhuri to 21.02% in Kalojira; against the control at 18.91%, 3 cultivars ranked higher, Kalojira being the highest. The means are given in Table 4.40 and plotted in Fig. 4.5.
1577: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. The year term was significant in 1 products and the year × cultivar term in 1, so that cultivar ranking held reasonably steady between years. Coefficients of variation lay between 0.91 and 3.19%, attesting to the precision of the trial. Amylose is deposited by granule-bound starch synthase I at the Waxy locus, and cultivars differ in the allele they carry. Cooking disorganises the granule but does not alter the quantity of amylose present.
1578: These results corroborate earlier reports. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) reported that apparent amylose governs eating and processing behaviour, and Tian et al. (2018) observed crystallinity and digestibility to decline without any change in amylose. Cheng et al. (2019) recorded that heat and moisture reconstitute the matrix into a firmer gel, and Devi and Badwaik (2022) demonstrated that amylose accounts for most of the varietal difference in cooking behaviour. The most favourable entry varied between products, Kalojira and Tulaipanji each ranking highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
1585: Starch constitutes the energy-supplying fraction of the grain and the basis of its texture; a higher value indicates a well-filled endosperm and good recovery of the edible fraction. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value in table rice at 28.07% and Kataribhog the lowest at 20.49%. The control returned 23.45%; 5 cultivars exceeded it, Radhunipagal most markedly. For khichdi the values lay between 34.24 and 42.72%, with the control at 38.36%; Lal Badshabhog ranked first, and 6 cultivars in all exceeded the control. In pulao the values ranged from 20.66 in Dudeshwar to 28.51% in Kataribhog; the control returned 20.66%, 8 cultivars exceeded that value and Kataribhog ranked first. Kalonunia recorded the highest value in payash at 24.22% and Tulaipanji the lowest at 16.57%; relative to 19.22% for the control, 4 cultivars were higher, Kalonunia being the best among them. Table 4.41 gives the means and Fig. 4.6 presents them graphically. The cultivars differed significantly in every product. The year effect was non-significant in every product, though the year × cultivar interaction was significant in 2, so that in those products the differences between cultivars were not of equal magnitude in both years. The coefficient of variation ranged from 2.30 to 2.68%, indicating reliable measurement.
